# Fix recommendations — experiment `f63b02a3c8ac`

**Target:** `things`  **Failure:** `container_pause`  **Generated by:** rules  
**Advisory only — nothing was applied.**

**Risk:** HIGH (6.2/10) — Pausing `things` (container_pause) moved API success from 100% to 0% across 24 samples; 1 service affected; recovered in 26 s without intervention. The safety monitor aborted early (error_rate).

_In production most users would see errors for the whole duration of a container_pause on things. Health checks stayed green while the API failed, so no orchestrator or alert would have reacted. The container sat unhealthy with nothing acting on it; Docker's restart policy does not cover this state._

## 1. Make readiness reflect subsystem health, and alert on /status/health

`configuration` · effort **M** · confidence 90%

In experiment f63b02a3c8ac (risk HIGH 6.2/10), API success fell to 0% during injection, TTR 26 s, findings: API success dropped to 0% during the fault; things-search kept reporting /ready=200 while the API was failing. The service kept answering `/ready` with 200 while the API was failing, so no orchestrator or alert could react. Ditto issue #1865 describes exactly this: the Pekko cluster was healthy but the persistence subsystem was not, and PR #1867 added a `subsystem-health` check under `management.health-checks.liveness-checks`.

**Steps**

1. Upgrade to a Ditto release containing PR #1867 (3.6+) and confirm `management.health-checks.liveness-checks.subsystem-health` is enabled.
2. Verify whether the equivalent subsystem check is wired into the readiness checks for your version; if not, add it (or treat `/status/health` as the readiness probe in compose/k8s instead of `/ready`).
3. Point the compose `healthcheck` of each Ditto service at `http://localhost:8558/status/health` (requires devops credentials or `DEVOPS_SECURED=false` in the lab) and fail on any `DOWN` component.
4. Add a Prometheus alert on `probe_success{job="ditto-health"} == 0` and on the API error-rate SLO, not only on `/alive`.

**Verify**

- Stop mongodb: within one healthcheck interval the Ditto services report `unhealthy` in `docker ps` and `/status/health` shows the persistence component `DOWN`.
- The `health_check_masked_failure` finding no longer appears when the experiment is replayed.

**References**

- https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto/issues/1865
- https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto/pull/1867
- https://eclipse.dev/ditto/installation-operating.html

## 2. Automate recovery after dependency outages: reconnect/backoff, health-keyed restarts, alert rule

`operations` · effort **M** · confidence 85%

In experiment f63b02a3c8ac (risk HIGH 6.2/10), API success fell to 0% during injection, TTR 26 s, findings: API success dropped to 0% during the fault; things-search kept reporting /ready=200 while the API was failing. The service did not come back on its own once its dependency returned; the injector had to restart it. Ditto discussion #1861 reports the same symptom (Things did not reconnect to MongoDB after an outage). In production this is a page at 03:00 for something a restart policy could do.

**Steps**

1. Review the Pekko persistence / Mongo driver reconnect settings for the affected service (restart-on-failure backoff in `ditto-*.conf`); make sure the persistence actors are restarted with exponential backoff rather than stopped after N failures.
2. Add a Docker healthcheck that hits `/status/health` and an `autoheal` sidecar (or Kubernetes liveness probe) so an `unhealthy` service is restarted automatically — `restart: always` ignores health state.
3. Add a Prometheus alert: `probe_success{instance=~"things|policies|gateway"} == 0 for 1m` and `rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[2m]) / rate(http_requests_total[2m]) > 0.05 for 2m`.
4. Document a runbook entry: 'if X is unhealthy after Mongo returns, `docker compose restart X`' until the automated path is proven.

**Verify**

- Replay the experiment; `recovery.remediation_actions` in the report must be empty and `recovered=true`.
- The alert fires in Prometheus/Alertmanager during the outage window.

**References**

- https://github.com/eclipse-ditto/ditto/discussions/1861
- https://github.com/willfarrell/docker-autoheal
- https://eclipse.dev/ditto/installation-operating.html

## 3. Scale things horizontally and make clients retry with idempotent, ETag-guarded writes

`architecture` · effort **M** · confidence 80%

In experiment f63b02a3c8ac (risk HIGH 6.2/10), API success fell to 0% during injection, TTR 26 s, findings: API success dropped to 0% during the fault; things-search kept reporting /ready=200 while the API was failing. Things actors are cluster-sharded, so a second instance lets Pekko re-home shards instead of waiting for the crashed JVM to restart. On the client side, every Thing write in Ditto is a PUT with `If-Match`/ETag support, so retries are safe and cheap.

**Steps**

1. Run `things` with `deploy.replicas: 2` (compose) or `replicas: 2` (k8s); keep the Pekko seed-node list stable.
2. Set a sensible `pekko.cluster.sharding.rebalance-interval` / `passivation` so shards move within a few seconds of a node loss.
3. In client SDKs, wrap PUT/PATCH with 3 retries + exponential backoff on 5xx/connection errors and send `If-Match: <etag>` to make the retry idempotent; treat 412 as 'already applied'.
4. Keep POST-created things (server-generated ids) behind a client-side idempotency key or prefer PUT with a client-chosen thingId.

**Verify**

- Kill one things instance: API success stays > 90% and the cluster view shows the shard regions rebalanced.
- A retried PUT with a stale `If-Match` returns 412 rather than overwriting newer state.

**References**

- https://eclipse.dev/ditto/httpapi-concepts.html
- https://eclipse.dev/ditto/installation-operating.html

## 4. Baseline observability: SLO alert rules and chaos annotations in Grafana

`observability` · effort **S** · confidence 65%

In experiment f63b02a3c8ac (risk HIGH 6.2/10), API success fell to 0% during injection, TTR 26 s, findings: API success dropped to 0% during the fault; things-search kept reporting /ready=200 while the API was failing. Whatever the specific fault, the first production improvement is knowing within a minute that users are affected. Alert on what the user sees (probe success, error rate, p95), not only on container liveness.

**Steps**

1. Prometheus rules: `probe_success == 0 for 1m` (blackbox on `/api/2/things` through nginx), API error-rate SLO burn (`sum(rate(requests{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests[5m])) > 0.02`), and `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) > 1s for 5m`.
2. Add a Grafana annotation (HTTP API `POST /api/annotations`, tag `chaos`) at the start and end of each Faultline experiment so latency spikes are attributable.
3. Dashboard the Docker health state per container (`container_health_status` via cAdvisor or a tiny exporter) next to the API SLIs.

**Verify**

- During the next experiment an alert fires within 60 s of the first API error and the Grafana graph shows the chaos window.

**References**

- https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/configuration/alerting_rules/
